Key highlights 1. Program introduction and Buildrathon orientation Nguyễn Gia Hưng introduced the program and the Buildrathon challenge. The kickoff provided context for the learning journey and the outcomes participants would work toward. The published event description also outlined the challenge’s objectives and judging criteria.
The presentation materials included an overview of AWS’s presence in Vietnam, organized around investment in local talent, infrastructure, and future skills. This gave the opening session a broader context for developing cloud and AI capabilities.
2. A practical example: an AI-enabled Slack bot The technical presentation showed a diagram labeled Market Slack Bot. The session explained an architecture through its connected components:
Component shown on the slide Detail illustrated in the diagram Slack Requests associated with mentions, direct messages, and active threads. Socket Mode / WebSocket The connection between Slack and the bot workflow. Response gate A response-control component positioned before Claude Code. Bot schedule, internal API, and cron + database Planned turns, application-owned jobs, and storage associated with memory and scheduled tasks. Open the Amazon VPC console In the navigation pane, choose Endpoints, then click Create Endpoint: You will see 6 existing VPC endpoints that support AWS Systems Manager (SSM). These endpoints were deployed automatically by the CloudFormation Templates for this workshop.

For Configure route tables, select the route table that is already associated with two subnets (note: this is not the main route table for the VPC, but a second route table created by CloudFormation). For Policy, leave the default option, Full Access, to allow full access to the service. You will deploy a VPC endpoint policy in a later lab module to demonstrate restricting access to S3 buckets based on policies. Do not add a tag to the VPC endpoint at this time. Click Create endpoint, then click x after receiving a successful creation message.

title: Introduction
content:
VPC endpoints VPC endpoints are virtual devices. They are horizontally scaled, redundant, and highly available VPC components. They allow communication between your compute resources and AWS services without imposing availability risks. Compute resources running in VPC can access Amazon S3 using a Gateway endpoint. PrivateLink interface endpoints can be used by compute resources running in VPC or on-premises. Workshop overview In this workshop, you will use two VPCs.
“VPC Cloud” is for cloud resources such as a Gateway endpoint and an EC2 instance to test with. “VPC On-Prem” simulates an on-premises environment such as a factory or corporate datacenter. An EC2 instance running strongSwan VPN software has been deployed in “VPC On-prem” and automatically configured to establish a Site-to-Site VPN tunnel with AWS Transit Gateway. This VPN simulates connectivity from an on-premises location to the AWS cloud. To minimize costs, only one VPN instance is provisioned to support this workshop. When planning VPN connectivity for your production workloads, AWS recommends using multiple VPN devices for high availability.

To finalize the VPN configuration, you will modify the “VPC On-prem” routing table to direct traffic destined for the cloud to the strongSwan VPN instance.
Open the Amazon EC2 console

title: Week 2 Worklog
content:
During the second week (September 21–25, 2026), I studied AWS networking and worked with VPC, EC2, and Route 53 Resolver. I recorded the work by day, moving from network fundamentals to Hybrid DNS testing and resource cleanup.
Week 2 objectives Understand how VPCs, CIDRs, subnets, and route tables are organized, and trace network traffic paths. Distinguish Security Groups from Network ACLs and consider both outbound and return traffic when checking connectivity. Build a public/private subnet environment, connect EC2 instances, and learn to manage private instances through an EC2 Instance Connect Endpoint. Compare VPC Peering, Transit Gateway, Site-to-Site VPN, Direct Connect, and load balancers at an architecture-selection level. Configure Hybrid DNS components with Route 53 Resolver and test domain-name resolution. Identify CloudFormation ownership boundaries and clean up resources according to their dependencies. Tasks completed this week Day Completed work Start date Completion date Learning sources Monday Studied VPC, CIDR, subnets, route tables, IGW, and NAT; distinguished Security Groups from Network ACLs; reviewed VPC Peering, Transit Gateway, Site-to-Site VPN, Direct Connect, and load balancers. 09/21/2026 09/21/2026 Module 02-01, 02-02, 02-03; VPC CIDR, Security Groups, Network ACLs Tuesday Reviewed subnet associations with route tables, the roles of IGW and NAT Gateway, Security Group and Network ACL rules, and how the VPC Resource Map helps visualize network components. 09/22/2026 09/22/2026 Module 02 playlist, videos 4–11; FCJ Lab03; Subnet sizing Wednesday Configured a sample 10.10.0.0/16 VPC with two public and two private subnets across two AZs, IGW, route tables, security groups, and EC2 instances; tested connectivity, NAT Gateway, and private EC2 access through EICE. 09/23/2026 09/23/2026 Module 02 playlist, videos 12–20; FCJ Lab03; EC2 Instance Connect Endpoint Thursday Prepared the Hybrid DNS environment with CloudFormation for the network and RDGW, configured the security group and RDGW access, and separately deployed Managed Microsoft AD following FCJ to simulate on-premises DNS. 09/24/2026 09/24/2026 Module 02 playlist, videos 21–25; FCJ CloudFormation, FCJ Managed AD Friday Configured a Route 53 outbound endpoint, a forwarding rule for onprem.example.com, and an inbound endpoint; tested DNS queries in the lab, then cleaned up endpoints, rules/associations, the directory, and the stack according to their ownership boundaries. 09/25/2026 09/25/2026 Module 02 playlist, videos 26–31; FCJ test results, FCJ cleanup; Outbound queries, Inbound queries Week 2 achievements Completed 31 Module 02, Lab03, and Lab10 videos; organized the material across five study days and connected concepts with the lab environments. Distinguished VPCs, subnets, route tables, IGW, NAT Gateway, Security Groups, and Network ACLs; understood how these components work together to route or control traffic. Configured a sample VPC with public/private subnets, EC2 instances, required routes, and tested the main connectivity paths in the lab. Learned to use an EC2 Instance Connect Endpoint to reach a private EC2 instance through its private IP, while recognizing that IAM, security groups, and routing still affect access. Configured Route 53 Resolver components for the Hybrid DNS lab and tested resolution for the simulated onprem.example.com domain. Cleaned up resources according to ownership: handling separately created components and resources managed by the CloudFormation stack. Lessons learned I learned to trace the full traffic path when analyzing connectivity: address and subnet, route table, network interface, security group, NACL, and destination service. A suitable route alone does not prove that a connection will succeed. I distinguished stateful Security Groups from stateless Network ACLs. When using a NACL, I need to consider rules for both outbound and return traffic, as well as rule evaluation order. I learned that public/private describes a subnet’s routing, while an EC2 instance’s public IP is a separate factor. I also concluded that CIDRs should be planned early to reduce conflicts when connecting networks; AWS allows secondary CIDRs to be associated under supported conditions. EICE helped me understand one way to manage a private EC2 instance through its private IP without assigning a public IP to the target. IAM permissions, security groups, and routing still need to be configured appropriately. I distinguished the query direction of Route 53 inbound and outbound endpoints. A successful query confirms only the path tested; each direction and application reachability need separate checks when the scope requires them. I learned that cleanup is part of the lab process. Before deleting resources, I need to identify which are managed by the stack and which were created separately, then handle them according to their dependencies. Next step In Week 3, I will move on to Multi-VPC, VPC Peering, and Transit Gateway, and study how to deploy and connect EC2 instances in a multi-network architecture.

Configured VPC Peering in the lab and identified the conditions required for connectivity between two VPCs, including non-overlapping CIDRs, routes on both sides, and suitable security rules. Built a multi-VPC Transit Gateway lab and distinguished VPC routes from TGW routes, including the roles of attachments, association, and propagation. Consolidated EC2 instance selection criteria and compared EBS and instance store data persistence across instance lifecycle actions. Distinguished User Data from instance metadata and reviewed the roles of Auto Scaling, EFS, FSx, Lightsail, and MGN. Lessons learned I learned that an active VPC Peering connection alone does not ensure application connectivity. I need to check CIDRs, routes on both sides, Security Groups, Network ACLs, and name resolution along the traffic path. I distinguished VPC route tables from TGW route tables. Association selects the TGW route table used for traffic arriving from an attachment, while propagation adds that attachment’s routes to the selected table. Reachability Analyzer helps me assess reachability based on network configuration; its result does not replace testing a running application connection. I learned that choosing EBS or instance store depends on performance and data-retention needs. Instance store is suited to temporary data, while data that must persist needs appropriate durable storage and lifecycle settings. I learned how AMIs and User Data support consistent instance initialization, while metadata provides instance information for operational processes. These concepts help me understand Auto Scaling designs. From the watch party, I took away that AI-assisted development needs appropriate access controls, test evidence, and accountable human review. Faster delivery still depends on reliable engineering foundations and validation. title: Week 4 Worklog
content:
During the fourth week (October 5–9, 2026), I worked through AWS Backup, S3 File Gateway, and S3/CloudFront labs, alongside the Module 04 storage lectures. I prepared the backup environment on Monday and completed its notification and restore-testing flow on Friday.
Week 4 objectives Configure AWS Backup policies and distinguish backup plans, vaults, resource assignments, and recovery points. Understand S3 File Gateway, SMB file shares, and the role of the local cache. Deploy an S3 static website and distribute its content through CloudFront with appropriate origin access permissions. Practice S3 Versioning, object movement, and Cross-Region Replication (CRR). Compare storage types, storage classes, lifecycle policies, CORS, and disaster recovery approaches. Complete backup notifications and restore checks, then clean up the lab resources. Tasks completed this week Day Completed work Start date Completion date Learning sources Monday Prepared S3 storage for the CloudFormation template and Lambda package, deployed the backup lab infrastructure, and configured a backup plan, rule, vault, and resource assignment. Reviewed the backup/restore flow and application recovery criteria for the checks later in the week. 10/05/2026 10/05/2026 FCJ Lab13: Introduction, S3 preparation, Infrastructure, Backup plan Tuesday Deployed S3 File Gateway on EC2, created an SMB file share, connected it to a Windows client, and checked that a file written through the share appeared in S3; cleaned up Lab24. Then created a separate S3 bucket, uploaded the website files, configured static website hosting and the lab’s public access settings, and checked the website endpoint. 10/06/2026 10/06/2026 FCJ Lab24 — Storage Gateway, Connect file share, Cleanup; FCJ Lab57: Create bucket, Upload data, Static website, Public access settings, Object permissions, Test website Wednesday Continued Lab57 by re-enabling S3 Block Public Access and configuring CloudFront with an S3 origin and bucket policy. Practiced versioning and version recovery, moving objects between buckets, and CRR; checked the distributed content and replication, then cleaned up the lab resources. 10/07/2026 10/07/2026 FCJ Lab57: Block public access, Configure CloudFront, Test CloudFront, Versioning, Move objects, Replication, Cleanup Thursday Studied block, file, and object storage; S3 Access Points, storage classes, lifecycle policies, CORS, and access permissions. Reviewed archive retrieval, hybrid and offline data transfer concepts, and disaster recovery strategies in relation to Recovery Time Objective (RTO) and Recovery Point Objective (RPO). 10/08/2026 10/08/2026 Module 04: Storage overview, S3, Access Points and storage classes, Static website, CORS and archive topics, Data transfer, Storage Gateway and Backup Friday Extended Monday’s backup environment by configuring Backup Vault Notifications through the AWS CLI and SNS. Created an on-demand backup and checked the lab’s Lambda-based restore and application validation flow through jobs, notifications, and CloudWatch Logs; completed resource cleanup. 10/09/2026 10/09/2026 FCJ Lab13: Notifications, Test restore, Cleanup Week 4 achievements Completed the learning material from 4 Module 04 videos and 26 FCJ pages, organized into five daily topic groups. Set up the AWS Backup lab and configured its plan, vault, and resource assignment; completed the notification and restore-testing flow at the end of the week. Configured an SMB file share through S3 File Gateway, checked the client-to-S3 write path, and cleaned up the gateway lab. Deployed an S3 static website and continued with CloudFront distribution and origin access configuration, distinguishing the two access paths. Practiced S3 version management, object movement, and CRR, and understood the purpose and scope of each mechanism. Consolidated storage selection and recovery criteria, including access patterns, retention, archive retrieval, and the distinction between CORS and access permissions. Lessons learned I learned that a completed backup job and successful application recovery are separate outcomes. Restore checks need criteria tied to the application’s behavior and data; a job status alone does not establish that RTO or RPO targets have been met. I distinguished file access through SMB from object access in S3. The gateway cache supports access to files, while changes made directly in S3 require consideration of the cache refresh mechanism. I understood that the ACL-based website exercise and the bucket policy used for CloudFront serve different access paths. Origin type and permissions must match how the content is intended to be accessed. I learned to check S3 versions and CDN caching separately. Recovering an object version does not by itself ensure that every client immediately receives that version through CloudFront. I understood that CRR asynchronously copies eligible objects according to its configuration. It does not replace the full backup and recovery strategy for an application. I learned to balance access patterns, retrieval time, retention, and RTO/RPO when choosing storage and recovery approaches. I also distinguished browser CORS settings from the permissions that authorize access to S3 objects. I learned to compare job states, notifications, and logs when reviewing a restore test. Cleanup also requires distinguishing stack-managed resources from separately created backup resources, stored data, and test resources. Next step In Week 5, I will continue with the next course modules and begin the project phase.

AWS Cloud and AI Day Hanoi 2026 — HCMC Watch Party
content:
Event information Item Details Event AWS Cloud and AI Day Hanoi 2026 Date September 29, 2026 Time 8:00 a.m.–5:00 p.m. (UTC+7) Format Ho Chi Minh City watch party following the program streamed from Hanoi Watch party venue 26th floor, Bitexco Financial Tower, 2 Hai Trieu Street, Saigon Ward, Ho Chi Minh City My role Attendee Event links AWS Cloud and AI Day Hanoi · Watch party information On September 29, 2026, I attended the AWS Cloud and AI Day Hanoi watch party in Ho Chi Minh City and followed the keynote streamed from Hanoi. The presentations explored how organizations are applying cloud and AI, the engineering foundations behind reliable services, and the need to validate software as AI takes on a larger role in development. These topics helped me connect new technologies with practical concerns such as security, reliability, and engineering accountability.
AWS promoted more than 30 sessions at the Hanoi event on agentic AI, data and analytics, application modernization, and industry solutions, alongside an expo and workshops. The watch party page listed the keynote and sessions from the Builders x AI track. This report focuses on the keynote, which is the portion covered by the transcript I provided.
Event objectives Learn how organizations in Vietnam are bringing cloud and AI into business processes. Understand the platform, security, and governance foundations needed to move AI beyond experimentation. Explore how AI-assisted development should be supported by testing, evidence, and accountable release decisions. Identify cloud and AI topics to study further through personal projects. Keynote speakers Order Speaker Title Main topic 1 Hoang Minh Deputy Minister of Science and Technology Digital infrastructure, compute capacity, and Vietnam’s cloud and AI ecosystem. 2 Jennifer Wicks U.S. Ambassador to Vietnam Technology cooperation and cloud’s role in digital transformation. 3 Eric Yeo Country General Manager Malaysia, Vietnam, Indochina, AWS Cloud and AI in Vietnam, customer examples, infrastructure, and skills development. 4 Dr. Jens Lottner Chief Executive Officer, Techcombank Integrating AI into enterprise workflows and developing staff capabilities. 5 Dr. Werner Vogels Chief Technology Officer, Amazon.com Invisible engineering, cloud foundations, and system design decisions. 6 Mai Le Director of Product Management, Katalon Software quality validation as AI accelerates development. AWS lists all six as keynote speakers. The transcript contains very little of Deputy Minister Hoang Minh’s opening remarks, so that part is supplemented by the Ministry of Science and Technology’s event report. The times below refer to the supplied keynote transcript.
Key highlights 1. Digital infrastructure and Vietnam’s cloud and AI ecosystem The opening remarks placed AI in a broader context: creating value from technology calls for digital infrastructure, compute capacity, skilled people, and collaboration. Deputy Minister Hoang Minh emphasized an ecosystem in which businesses, government, universities, and research organizations contribute to developing technology. Ambassador Jennifer Wicks spoke about cloud’s role in innovation, competitiveness, and technology cooperation between Vietnam and the United States. Source for the Deputy Minister’s remarks: Ministry of Science and Technology.
2. Cloud and AI applications tied to customer needs Eric Yeo presented customer examples showing how AI can support concrete activities, including healthcare information analysis, in-store product display monitoring, and agricultural operations. My takeaway is to start with the problem to solve, then consider the data, cloud services, and measures needed to evaluate the result. He also discussed the Hanoi AWS Local Zone as an infrastructure option closer to local users. AWS had announced the Local Zone’s availability in June 2026, before this event.
3. Techcombank: integrating AI into workflows Dr. Jens Lottner described AI as a way to change how work is organized, rather than simply add a standalone tool. Examples included coordinating software requirements, development, and testing; using an agent to connect operations and customer service when resolving incidents; and helping frontline staff prepare information for customers.
The presentation also highlighted orchestration platforms, access governance, model selection, staff training, and outcome measurement. The name of one software development tool is unclear in the transcript, so I have described its role without assigning an unverified product name. These examples and any reported improvements belong to the speaker’s presentation; they are not systems I implemented.
4. Werner Vogels: the invisible engineering behind services Dr. Werner Vogels used database and infrastructure stories to explain the engineering decisions that end users often do not see. One lesson was to understand how an application accesses data before choosing an architecture. Sound design starts with real requirements and access patterns.
Cloud examples illustrated several layers of this work: the AWS Nitro System supports infrastructure operations; Lambda and Firecracker illustrate event-driven workloads in isolated environments; and Lambda SnapStart uses snapshots of initialized environments to improve startup performance for supported runtimes. The discussion of the Amazon Time Sync Service and ClockBound extended the topic to time in distributed systems: timestamps need uncertainty information so applications can reason about event ordering. AWS Lambda SnapStart documentation · AWS ClockBound.
This session helped me see how cloud services depend on engineering choices involving performance, isolation, time, and reliability. Understanding these foundations helps engineers select solutions based on system requirements instead of relying on service names alone.
5. Katalon: validation must keep pace with software development Mai Le described the validation gap between AI-assisted development speed and the ability to test software. When code and changes are produced faster than they can be assessed, risk can reach users. An AI agent therefore needs connected context from requirements, code changes, test cases, defects, and operational data to determine what should be tested.
In Katalon’s platform example, the speaker mentioned Amazon EKS, Amazon RDS, Amazon S3, and Amazon Kinesis as the foundation for its application, data, and telemetry; Amazon Bedrock for governed model access; and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime as an isolated environment for agents and approved tools. The key point was that a confident AI answer does not prove that software works. Teams need test results, logs, screenshots, videos, and telemetry. People still define risk boundaries, review exceptions, and decide whether to release. References: Katalon True Platform · AWS AgentCore Runtime.
6. Validation debt and engineering accountability In the closing remarks, Werner Vogels returned to validation debt: the work that accumulates when software changes are produced faster than they can be verified. I took away the need to pair development speed with disciplined testing, traceable evidence, and clear responsibility. Foundation work may be invisible to users, but it contributes to more dependable software.
Key takeaways Start with the problem: define the workflow, users, and intended outcome before choosing an AI model or service. Design governance into the architecture: agents need appropriate permissions, defined tools, and observable activity. Validate output with evidence: tests, logs, and telemetry help teams assess what actually happened. Understand engineering trade-offs: performance, isolation, cost, and reliability all matter when designing a system. Keep people accountable: AI can assist with development and testing, while engineers remain responsible for evaluating risk and release decisions. Next steps I plan to choose a small use case for practicing an AI-assisted workflow. Before testing it, I will define its inputs and outputs, set limits on tool access, write validation criteria, and retain logs and results for review. This is a future learning plan, not hands-on work completed at the watch party.
Watch party experience I attended the AWS Cloud and AI Day through the Ho Chi Minh City watch party and followed the keynote streamed from Hanoi. It gave me a way to learn from AWS, business leaders, and product specialists alongside the local builder community. title: Proposal
content:
⚠️ Note: The information below is for reference purposes only. Please do not copy verbatim for your report, including this warning.
In this section, you need to summarize the contents of the workshop that you plan to conduct.
IoT Weather Platform for Lab Research A Unified AWS Serverless Solution for Real-Time Weather Monitoring 1. Executive Summary The IoT Weather Platform is designed for the ITea Lab team in Ho Chi Minh City to enhance weather data collection and analysis. It supports up to 5 weather stations, with potential scalability to 10-15, utilizing Raspberry Pi edge devices with ESP32 sensors to transmit data via MQTT. The platform leverages AWS Serverless services to deliver real-time monitoring, predictive analytics, and cost efficiency, with access restricted to 5 lab members via Amazon Cognito.
2. Problem Statement What’s the Problem? Current weather stations require manual data collection, becoming unmanageable with multiple units. There is no centralized system for real-time data or analytics, and third-party platforms are costly and overly complex.
The Solution The platform uses AWS IoT Core to ingest MQTT data, AWS Lambda and API Gateway for processing, Amazon S3 for storage (including a data lake), and AWS Glue Crawlers and ETL jobs to extract, transform, and load data from the S3 data lake to another S3 bucket for analysis. AWS Amplify with Next.js provides the web interface, and Amazon Cognito ensures secure access. Similar to Thingsboard and CoreIoT, users can register new devices and manage connections, though this platform operates on a smaller scale and is designed for private use. Key features include real-time dashboards, trend analysis, and low operational costs.
Benefits and Return on Investment The solution establishes a foundational resource for lab members to develop a larger IoT platform, serving as a study resource, and provides a data foundation for AI enthusiasts for model training or analysis. It reduces manual reporting for each station via a centralized platform, simplifying management and maintenance, and improves data reliability. Monthly costs are $0.66 USD per the AWS Pricing Calculator, with a 12-month total of $7.92 USD. All IoT equipment costs are covered by the existing weather station setup, eliminating additional development expenses. The break-even period of 6-12 months is achieved through significant time savings from reduced manual work.
3. Solution Architecture The platform employs a serverless AWS architecture to manage data from 5 Raspberry Pi-based stations, scalable to 15. Data is ingested via AWS IoT Core, stored in an S3 data lake, and processed by AWS Glue Crawlers and ETL jobs to transform and load it into another S3 bucket for analysis. Lambda and API Gateway handle additional processing, while Amplify with Next.js hosts the dashboard, secured by Cognito. The architecture is detailed below:
AWS Services Used AWS IoT Core: Ingests MQTT data from 5 stations, scalable to 15. AWS Lambda: Processes data and triggers Glue jobs (two functions). Amazon API Gateway: Facilitates web app communication. Amazon S3: Stores raw data in a data lake and processed outputs (two buckets). AWS Glue: Crawlers catalog data, and ETL jobs transform and load it. AWS Amplify: Hosts the Next.js web interface. Amazon Cognito: Secures access for lab users. Component Design Edge Devices: Raspberry Pi collects and filters sensor data, sending it to IoT Core. Data Ingestion: AWS IoT Core receives MQTT messages from the edge devices. Data Storage: Raw data is stored in an S3 data lake; processed data is stored in another S3 bucket. Data Processing: AWS Glue Crawlers catalog the data, and ETL jobs transform it for analysis. Web Interface: AWS Amplify hosts a Next.js app for real-time dashboards and analytics. User Management: Amazon Cognito manages user access, allowing up to 5 active accounts. 4. Technical Implementation Implementation Phases This project has two parts—setting up weather edge stations and building the weather platform—each following 4 phases:
Build Theory and Draw Architecture: Research Raspberry Pi setup with ESP32 sensors and design the AWS serverless architecture (1 month pre-internship) Calculate Price and Check Practicality: Use AWS Pricing Calculator to estimate costs and adjust if needed (Month 1). Fix Architecture for Cost or Solution Fit: Tweak the design (e.g., optimize Lambda with Next.js) to stay cost-effective and usable (Month 2). Develop, Test, and Deploy: Code the Raspberry Pi setup, AWS services with CDK/SDK, and Next.js app, then test and release to production (Months 2-3). Technical Requirements
Weather Edge Station: Sensors (temperature, humidity, rainfall, wind speed), a microcontroller (ESP32), and a Raspberry Pi as the edge device. Raspberry Pi runs Raspbian, handles Docker for filtering, and sends 1 MB/day per station via MQTT over Wi-Fi. Weather Platform: Practical knowledge of AWS Amplify (hosting Next.js), Lambda (minimal use due to Next.js), AWS Glue (ETL), S3 (two buckets), IoT Core (gateway and rules), and Cognito (5 users). Use AWS CDK/SDK to code interactions (e.g., IoT Core rules to S3). Next.js reduces Lambda workload for the fullstack web app. 5. Timeline & Milestones Project Timeline
Pre-Internship (Month 0): 1 month for planning and old station review. Internship (Months 1-3): 3 months. Month 1: Study AWS and upgrade hardware. Month 2: Design and adjust architecture. Month 3: Implement, test, and launch. Post-Launch: Up to 1 year for research. 6. Budget Estimation You can find the budget estimation on the AWS Pricing Calculator.
Or you can download the Budget Estimation File.
Infrastructure Costs AWS Services: AWS Lambda: $0.00/month (1,000 requests, 512 MB storage). S3 Standard: $0.15/month (6 GB, 2,100 requests, 1 GB scanned). Data Transfer: $0.02/month (1 GB inbound, 1 GB outbound). AWS Amplify: $0.35/month (256 MB, 500 ms requests). Amazon API Gateway: $0.01/month (2,000 requests). AWS Glue ETL Jobs: $0.02/month (2 DPUs). AWS Glue Crawlers: $0.07/month (1 crawler). MQTT (IoT Core): $0.08/month (5 devices, 45,000 messages). Total: $0.7/month, $8.40/12 months
Hardware: $265 one-time (Raspberry Pi 5 and sensors). 7. Risk Assessment Risk Matrix Network Outages: Medium impact, medium probability. Sensor Failures: High impact, low probability. Cost Overruns: Medium impact, low probability. Mitigation Strategies Network: Local storage on Raspberry Pi with Docker. Sensors: Regular checks and spares. Cost: AWS budget alerts and optimization. Contingency Plans Revert to manual methods if AWS fails. Use CloudFormation for cost-related rollbacks. 8. Expected Outcomes Technical Improvements: Real-time data and analytics replace manual processes.
Scalable to 10-15 stations.
Long-term Value 1-year data foundation for AI research.
Reusable for future projects.

Connect to EC2 with session manager For this workshop, you will use AWS Session Manager to access several EC2 instances. Session Manager is a fully managed AWS Systems Manager capability that allows you to manage your Amazon EC2 instances and on-premises virtual machines (VMs) through an interactive one-click browser-based shell. Session Manager provides secure and auditable instance management without the need to open inbound ports, maintain bastion hosts, or manage SSH keys.
First Cloud AI Journey Lab for indepth understanding of Session manager.
In the AWS Management Console, start typing Systems Manager in the quick search box and press Enter: From the Systems Manager menu, find Node Management in the left menu and click Session Manager: Click Start Session, and select the EC2 instance named Test-Gateway-Endpoint. This EC2 instance is already running in “VPC Cloud” and will be used to test connectivity to Amazon S3 through the Gateway endpoint you just created (s3-gwe).
Session Manager will open a new browser tab with a shell prompt: sh-4.2 $
You have successfully start a session - connect to the EC2 instance in VPC cloud. In the next step, we will create a S3 bucket and a file in it.
Create a file and upload to s3 bucket Change to the ssm-user’s home directory by typing cd ~ in the CLI Create a new file to use for testing with the command fallocate -l 1G testfile.xyz, which will create a file of 1GB size named “testfile.xyz”. Upload file to S3 bucket with command aws s3 cp testfile.xyz s3://your-bucket-name. Replace your-bucket-name with the name of S3 bucket that you created earlier. You have successfully uploaded the file to your S3 bucket. You can now terminate the session.
Check object in S3 bucket Navigate to S3 console. Click the name of your s3 bucket In the Bucket console, you will see the file you have uploaded to your S3 bucket Section summary Congratulation on completing access to S3 from VPC. In this section, you created a Gateway endpoint for Amazon S3, and used the AWS CLI to upload an object. The upload worked because the Gateway endpoint allowed communication to S3, without needing an Internet Gateway attached to “VPC Cloud”. This demonstrates the functionality of the Gateway endpoint as a secure path to S3 without traversing the Public Internet.

title: Access S3 from on-premises
content:
Overview In this section, you will create an Interface endpoint to access Amazon S3 from a simulated on-premises environment. The Interface endpoint will allow you to route to Amazon S3 over a VPN connection from your simulated on-premises environment.
Why using Interface endpoint:
Gateway endpoints only work with resources running in the VPC where they are created. Interface endpoints work with resources running in VPC, and also resources running in on-premises environments. Connectivty from your on-premises environment to the cloud can be provided by AWS Site-to-Site VPN or AWS Direct Connect. Interface endpoints allow you to connect to services powered by AWS PrivateLink. These services include some AWS services, services hosted by other AWS customers and partners in their own VPCs (referred to as PrivateLink Endpoint Services), and supported AWS Marketplace Partner services. For this workshop, we will focus on connecting to Amazon S3.

title: On-premises DNS Simulation
content:
AWS PrivateLink endpoints have a fixed IP address in each Availability Zone where they are deployed, for the life of the endpoint (until it is deleted). These IP addresses are attached to Elastic Network Interfaces (ENIs). AWS recommends using DNS to resolve the IP addresses for endpoints so that downstream applications use the latest IP addresses when ENIs are added to new AZs, or deleted over time.
In this section, you will create a forwarding rule to send DNS resolution requests from a simulated on-premises environment to a Route 53 Private Hosted Zone. This section leverages the infrastructure deployed by CloudFormation in the Prepare the environment section.
Create DNS Alias Records for the Interface endpoint Navigate to the Route 53 management console (Hosted Zones section). The CloudFormation template you deployed in the Prepare the environment section created this Private Hosted Zone. Click on the name of the Private Hosted Zone, s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com: Create a new record in the Private Hosted Zone: Record name and record type keep default options Alias Button: Click to enable Route traffic to: Alias to VPC Endpoint Region: US East (N. Virginia) [us-east-1] Choose endpoint: Paste the Regional VPC Endpoint DNS name from your text editor (you saved when doing section 4.3) Click Add another record, and add a second record using the following values. Click Create records when finished to create both records. Record name: *. Record type: keep default value (type A) Alias Button: Click to enable Route traffic to: Alias to VPC Endpoint Region: US East (N. Virginia) [us-east-1] Choose endpoint: Paste the Regional VPC Endpoint DNS name from your text editor The new records appear in the Route 53 console:
Create a Resolver Forwarding Rule Route 53 Resolver Forwarding Rules allow you to forward DNS queries from your VPC to other sources for name resolution. Outside of a workshop environment, you might use this feature to forward DNS queries from your VPC to DNS servers running on-premises. In this section, you will simulate an on-premises conditional forwarder by creating a forwarding rule that forwards DNS queries for Amazon S3 to a Private Hosted Zone running in “VPC Cloud” in-order to resolve the PrivateLink interface endpoint regional DNS name.
From the Route 53 management console, click Inbound endpoints on the left side bar In the Inbound endpoints console, click the ID of the inbound endpoint Copy the two IP addresses listed to your text editor From the Route 53 menu, choose Resolver > Rules, and click Create rule: In the Create rule console: Name: myS3Rule Rule type: Forward Domain name: s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com VPC: VPC On-prem Outbound endpoint: VPCOnpremOutboundEndpoint Target IP Addresses: Enter both IP addresses from your text editor (inbound endpoint addresses) and then click Submit You have successfully created resolver forwarding rule.
Test the on-premises DNS Simulation Connect to Test-Interface-Endpoint EC2 instance with Session manager Test DNS resolution. The dig command will return the IP addresses assigned to the VPC Interface endpoint running in VPC Cloud (your IP’s will be different): dig +short s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com The IP addresses returned are the VPC endpoint IP addresses, NOT the Resolver IP addresses you pasted from your text editor. The IP addresses of the Resolver endpoint and the VPC endpoint look similar because they are all from the VPC Cloud CIDR block.
Navigate to the VPC menu (Endpoints section), select the S3 Interface endpoint. Click the Subnets tab and verify that the IP addresses returned by Dig match the VPC endpoint: Return to your shell and use the AWS CLI to test listing your S3 buckets: aws s3 ls --endpoint-url https://s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com Terminate your Session Manager session: In this section you created an Interface endpoint for Amazon S3. This endpoint can be reached from on-premises through Site-to-Site VPN or AWS Direct Connect. Route 53 Resolver outbound endpoints simulated forwarding DNS requests from on-premises to a Private Hosted Zone running the cloud. Route 53 inbound Endpoints recieved the resolution request and returned a response containing the IP addresses of the VPC interface endpoint. Using DNS to resolve the endpoint IP addresses provides high availability in-case of an Availability Zone outage.

title: VPC Endpoint Policies
content:
When you create an interface or gateway endpoint, you can attach an endpoint policy to it that controls access to the service to which you are connecting. A VPC endpoint policy is an IAM resource policy that you attach to an endpoint. If you do not attach a policy when you create an endpoint, AWS attaches a default policy for you that allows full access to the service through the endpoint.
You can create a policy that restricts access to specific S3 buckets only. This is useful if you only want certain S3 Buckets to be accessible through the endpoint.
In this section you will create a VPC endpoint policy that restricts access to the S3 bucket specified in the VPC endpoint policy.
Connect to an EC2 instance and verify connectivity to S3 Start a new AWS Session Manager session on the instance named Test-Gateway-Endpoint. From the session, verify that you can list the contents of the bucket you created in Part 1: Access S3 from VPC: aws s3 ls s3://\<your-bucket-name\> The bucket contents include the two 1 GB files uploaded in earlier.
Create a new S3 bucket; follow the naming pattern you used in Part 1, but add a ‘-2’ to the name. Leave other fields as default and click create Successfully create bucket
Navigate to: Services > VPC > Endpoints, then select the Gateway VPC endpoint you created earlier. Click the Policy tab. Click Edit policy. The default policy allows access to all S3 Buckets through the VPC endpoint.
In Edit Policy console, copy & Paste the following policy, then replace yourbucketname-2 with your 2nd bucket name. This policy will allow access through the VPC endpoint to your new bucket, but not any other bucket in Amazon S3. Click Save to apply the policy. { "Id": "Policy1631305502445", "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Sid": "Stmt1631305501021", "Action": "s3:*", "Effect": "Allow", "Resource": [ "arn:aws:s3:::yourbucketname-2", "arn:aws:s3:::yourbucketname-2/*" ], "Principal": "*" } ] } Successfully customize policy
From your session on the Test-Gateway-Endpoint instance, test access to the S3 bucket you created in Part 1: Access S3 from VPC aws s3 ls s3://<yourbucketname> This command will return an error because access to this bucket is not permitted by your new VPC endpoint policy:
Return to your home directory on your EC2 instance cd~ Create a file fallocate -l 1G test-bucket2.xyz Copy file to 2nd bucket aws s3 cp test-bucket2.xyz s3://<your-2nd-bucket-name> This operation succeeds because it is permitted by the VPC endpoint policy.
Then we test access to the first bucket by copy the file to 1st bucket aws s3 cp test-bucket2.xyz s3://<your-1st-bucket-name> This command will return an error because access to this bucket is not permitted by your new VPC endpoint policy.
Part 3 Summary: In this section, you created a VPC endpoint policy for Amazon S3, and used the AWS CLI to test the policy. AWS CLI actions targeted to your original S3 bucket failed because you applied a policy that only allowed access to the second bucket you created. AWS CLI actions targeted for your second bucket succeeded because the policy allowed them. These policies can be useful in situations where you need to control access to resources through VPC endpoints.

Gateway - Create a gateway endpoint to send traffic to Amazon S3 or DynamoDB using private IP addresses.You route traffic from your VPC to the gateway endpoint using route tables. Interface - Create an interface endpoint to send traffic to endpoint services that use a Network Load Balancer to distribute traffic. Traffic destined for the endpoint service is resolved using DNS.
